core: Case management as a coordinating function that connects a person to services held by different organizations, distinct from counseling and from direct provision of the underlying service
The phases - engagement, assessment, planning, linkage and coordination, monitoring, advocacy, transition or closure - and why they operate as a cycle rather than a one-way pipeline
The model family and its structural differences: brokerage/generalist, clinical/therapeutic, strengths model, assertive community treatment, intensive case management
Evidence differing sharply by model: intensive case management and ACT versus generic case management, with effect sizes and certainty ratings
Caseload size as the variable that most often determines whether a model can run as designed, and the caseload/workload distinction
Documentation's dual role as clinical record and legal/financial record
Interdisciplinary teams and the coordination problem the function exists to solve
Case management as practiced versus as funded: Medicaid targeted case management rules and what they permit a case manager to bill for
Rigor point: case management is not paperwork with a nicer name and is not therapy
Rigor point: evidence for ACT is not evidence for brokerage
Rigor point: the person is not the case; the field's terminology is under active revision and word choice measurably affects professional judgment

claims.claim: Professional and regulatory definitions of case management describe a coordinating function: planning, seeking, advocating for, and monitoring services from different organizations on a person's behalf, in order to limit the harm caused by service fragmentation, staff turnover, and poor coordination among providers.

Federal treatment guidance identifies five core case management functions - assessment, planning, linkage, monitoring, and advocacy - and defines advocacy as ensuring services fit the person's needs rather than requiring the person to fit the available services.

Federal treatment guidance distinguishes four case management models - broker/generalist, assertive community treatment, strengths-based, and clinical/rehabilitation - which differ in the length and intensity of the relationship, caseload size, whether outreach is assertive, whether the caseload is shared by a team, and whether the same professional also provides therapy.

The difference between case management and therapy is one of emphasis: case management stresses acquiring resources while therapy focuses on intrapersonal and interpersonal change, and people frequently need both.

Federal Medicaid regulation defines case management services as services that assist eligible individuals in gaining access to needed medical, social, educational, and other services, and lists the activities as comprehensive assessment, development of a specific care plan, referral and related activities including scheduling appointments, and monitoring and follow-up conducted at least annually.

Federal financial participation is not available for case management activities that are in fact the direct delivery of the underlying medical, educational, or social service to which a person was referred; the regulation also requires free choice among qualified providers, prohibits duplicate payment, and bars making case management compulsory or a condition of receiving other services.

Assertive community treatment is defined by structural features rather than by philosophy: a multidisciplinary team, in vivo (community-based) service delivery, a caseload ratio of ten people per staff member, a shared caseload carried by the team, daily team meetings, twenty-four-hour seven-day availability, and services provided for as long as needed.

The 2017 Cochrane review of intensive case management included 40 randomized trials and 7,524 participants and defined intensive case management by a caseload of fewer than 20 people per worker plus high-intensity input, with non-intensive case management defined as the same package delivered at caseloads above 20.

Compared with standard care, intensive case management slightly reduced days in hospital per month (MD -0.86, 95% CI -1.37 to -0.34; 24 RCTs; low-quality evidence) and reduced the number of people leaving the trial early (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.58 to 0.79; 13 RCTs; low-quality evidence).

Compared with non-intensive case management, intensive case management probably makes little or no difference to average days in hospital per month (MD -0.08, 95% CI -0.37 to 0.21; 21 RCTs; moderate-quality evidence).

In the review's meta-regression, greater fidelity to the original ACT team organization was associated with greater reduction in time in hospital (coefficient -0.36, 95% CI -0.66 to -0.07) and higher baseline hospital use in the study setting was likewise associated with greater reduction (coefficient -0.20, 95% CI -0.32 to -0.10); with both variables in the model, organisation fidelity was no longer significant while baseline hospital use remained so.

A Cochrane review of non-intensive case management reported that case management approximately doubled the number of people admitted to psychiatric hospital (OR 1.84, 99% CI 1.33 to 2.57, n = 1,300) while increasing contact with services, and concluded it did not produce clinically significant improvement in mental state, social functioning, or quality of life; that review and the companion Cochrane review of assertive community treatment were both withdrawn from publication in 2011 as out of date.

A review of 75 studies concluded that ACT and intensive case management reduce time in hospital and improve housing stability, especially among high users of services, show little effect on social functioning, arrests, or vocational functioning, and that gains deteriorate when the services are reduced or withdrawn.

In substance use services, a review of 48 studies distinguished intensive case management, assertive community treatment, strengths-based case management, and generalist case management, finding ICM and ACT effective for homeless and dually diagnosed populations and strengths-based and generalist models relatively effective more generally, with mixed results on drug use and psychosocial functioning.

Evidence for the strengths model of case management is emerging rather than settled: a critical review of seven intervention studies reported improvements in hospitalization, employment and education, and intrapersonal outcomes while calling for higher-quality research, and a meta-analysis pooling five studies with 194 participants found no significant effect on level of functioning or quality of life.

Professional standards distinguish caseload (the number of people served at a given time) from workload (all functions performed in support of the service), state that workload sustainability cannot be judged from caseload size alone because model, complexity, resources, administrative duties and technology all matter, and state that caseload size directly affects a worker's capacity to engage people and that organizations must set policies maintaining reasonable caseloads.

Case management documentation serves clinical purposes (communication with other providers, continuity, service planning, practice and program evaluation) and simultaneously serves reimbursement, utilization review, organizational accountability to funders, and support for the practitioner in the event of a legal review; federal rules separately require records of the dates and nature of services and progress toward care plan goals.

Terminology for the people served varies by setting and funder - client, beneficiary, consumer, patient, peer, resident - and current state program standards require person-centered language; a randomized study found that clinicians reading an otherwise identical vignette assigned more personal blame and endorsed more punitive responses when the person was labeled a 'substance abuser' rather than described as having a substance use disorder, a finding federal guidance now builds on.

Interdisciplinary and interorganizational collaboration is treated as a professional standard in its own right, and ACT operationalizes it through a shared caseload and daily team meetings covering hospitalizations, incarcerations, risk situations, and emerging needs.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether case management as a category 'works'
positions: Older Cochrane evidence found that non-intensive case management increased psychiatric admissions without improving mental state, social functioning, or quality of life
The 2017 Cochrane review found intensive case management slightly better than standard care on days in hospital and clearly better on retention in care
The same 2017 review found intensive case management probably no better than non-intensive case management on days in hospital
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson does not deliver a verdict on the category. It reports the comparisons separately, attaches the certainty ratings, and teaches the general rule that evidence attaches to a specified structure (team, caseload, availability) rather than to the job title. The older reviews are labelled as withdrawn and therefore historical.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether fidelity to the ACT model or the baseline hospital use of the population explains ICM's advantage
positions: Organisation fidelity to ACT predicted greater reduction in time in hospital in single-variable meta-regression
When organisation fidelity and baseline hospital use were entered together, only baseline hospital use remained significant
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both results are stated. The lesson uses fidelity as the reason a renamed program cannot claim ACT's evidence, while explicitly noting the combined-model result as a caution against treating either variable as a simple causal lever.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether case management excludes clinical work
positions: Regulatory and brokerage framings treat coordination and the underlying service as separate, and Medicaid will not fund the underlying service as case management
Clinical case management and ACT deliberately combine coordination with treatment in the same worker or team
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the general boundary (coordination is the defining task) and then names clinical case management and ACT as designs that combine the roles on purpose - which is why they are named as distinct models rather than treated as the default.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained no substantive claims about case management at all - only placeholder language asserting that the topic is 'a foundational concept' students use 'to organize information'.
The draft's vocabulary list defined the topic in terms of itself and offered generic entries (context, evidence, application) unrelated to case management practice.
The draft's Eli-10 analogy (a label on a toolbox drawer) described nothing about coordination, caseload, or service systems.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire generated draft with researched content; no boilerplate wording was retained.
Added the coordination-versus-direct-service boundary and its regulatory enforcement, which the draft did not contain.
Added model-specific evidence with effect estimates and GRADE certainty, replacing the draft's absence of any evidential content.
Added caseload, documentation, team, and funding constraints as the operating conditions of the role.
Added an explicit educational-material statement and pointers to the two parallel unit topics that own assessment method and the referral process.

sourceRecords.title: NASW Standards for Social Work Case Management (2013)
sourceRecords.notes: Primary source for the profession's definition of case management (planning, seeking, advocating for, and monitoring services across organizations to limit fragmentation), the twelve standards and their titles, Standard 8 on interdisciplinary and interorganizational collaboration, Standard 10 on record keeping (clinical continuity, reimbursement and utilization review, support in the event of legal review, and the listed record elements), Standard 11 on workload sustainability (caseload versus workload; the variables that make a caseload number uninterpretable on its own; organizational responsibility), and the note that terminology for the people served varies by setting and funder. Copyright (c) 2013 NASW, all rights reserved; read via local PDF text extraction and restated in original wording.

sourceRecords.title: Substance Abuse and Case Management: An Introduction, Chapter 1 of Comprehensive Case Management for Substance Abuse Treatment (Treatment Improvement Protocol Series, No. 27)
sourceRecords.provider: Center for Substance Abuse Treatment, Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (U.S. Department of Health and Human Services), 2000; read on NCBI Bookshelf
sourceRecords.notes: Federal treatment guidance, public domain. Supports the five core functions used in the lesson (assessment, planning, linkage, monitoring, advocacy) including its framing of advocacy as making services fit the person rather than the reverse; the four-model taxonomy (broker/generalist, assertive community treatment, strengths-based, clinical/rehabilitation) with each model's distinguishing features - the broker model's limited, time-bounded relationship and larger caseloads, ACT's outreach, manageable caseloads, frequent contact, team-shared caseload and long-term commitment, the strengths model's focus on assets and informal networks, and the clinical/rehabilitation model's combination of therapy and case management in one professional; and the distinction that case management stresses resource acquisition while therapy focuses on intrapersonal and interpersonal change, with most people needing both. Published in 2000: used for definitions, functions, and model structure only, never for current effect estimates.

sourceRecords.title: What is a Case Manager?
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the cross-professional definition of case management as a collaborative process of assessment, planning facilitation, care coordination, evaluation, and advocacy for options and services, and the framing of the case manager as the communication hub connecting a person with providers and community resources. Used to show that the coordination definition is not specific to social work. No licence statement on the page; paraphrased only.

sourceRecords.title: 42 CFR 440.169 - Case management services
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Government (Code of Federal Regulations), text read on the Legal Information Institute mirror, Cornell Law School
sourceRecords.notes: Regulatory definition of case management services (assisting eligible individuals in gaining access to needed medical, social, educational and other services) and of targeted case management, plus the four listed activities: comprehensive assessment and periodic reassessment, development of a specific care plan stating goals and actions, referral and related activities including scheduling appointments, and monitoring and follow-up performed at least annually. Federal regulation text is public domain; LII's own annotations are copyrighted and were not used.

sourceRecords.title: 42 CFR 441.18 - Case management services (conditions for federal financial participation)
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Government (Code of Federal Regulations), text read on the Legal Information Institute mirror, Cornell Law School
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the practiced-versus-funded section: FFP is unavailable for case management activities that are the direct delivery of the underlying medical, educational, or social service (with child-welfare examples including transportation and home investigations); states must permit free choice among qualified providers; payments may not duplicate other payments; case management may not be compulsory or a condition of receiving other services; providers must maintain records of dates, nature of services, and progress toward care plan goals. Federal regulation text is public domain.

sourceRecords.title: Intensive case management for severe mental illness (Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 2017, Issue 1, Art. No. CD007906)
sourceRecords.provider: Dieterich M, Irving CB, Bergman H, Khokhar MA, Park B, Marshall M / The Cochrane Collaboration, published by John Wiley & Sons; published version deposited in White Rose Research Online (University of York)
sourceRecords.notes: Read in full via local PDF text extraction of the abstract, plain language summary, and authors' conclusions. Supports: 40 RCTs and 7,524 participants; ICM defined by caseloads under 20 with high-intensity input and 24-hour availability, non-ICM defined by caseloads above 20; ICM versus standard care MD -0.86 days in hospital per month (95% CI -1.37 to -0.34, 24 RCTs, low quality) and RR 0.68 for leaving the trial early (95% CI 0.58 to 0.79, 13 RCTs, low quality); ICM versus non-ICM MD -0.08 days per month (95% CI -0.37 to 0.21, 21 RCTs, moderate quality); meta-regression coefficients for organisation fidelity (-0.36, 95% CI -0.66 to -0.07) and baseline hospital use (-0.20, 95% CI -0.32 to -0.10), with only baseline hospital use remaining significant when combined; authors' conclusion that ICM is most valuable where baseline hospitalisation is around four days per month. Copyright Cochrane/Wiley; numerical findings restated in original wording, no prose reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: WITHDRAWN: Case management for people with severe mental disorders (Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, CD000050.pub2)
sourceRecords.provider: Marshall M, Gray A, Lockwood A, Green R / The Cochrane Collaboration; bibliographic record and abstract retrieved through the Europe PMC REST API (EMBL-EBI)
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the historical finding that non-intensive case management approximately doubled the number of people admitted to psychiatric hospital (OR 1.84, 99% CI 1.33 to 2.57, n = 1,300) while increasing service contact, and the authors' conclusion that it produced no clinically significant improvement in mental state, social functioning, or quality of life. The record's title begins 'WITHDRAWN:', confirming the review was withdrawn from the Cochrane Library in 2011; the lesson labels it historical rather than current. Abstract only; no text reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: WITHDRAWN: Assertive community treatment for people with severe mental disorders (Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, CD001089.pub2)
sourceRecords.provider: Marshall M, Lockwood A / The Cochrane Collaboration; bibliographic record retrieved through the Europe PMC REST API (EMBL-EBI)
sourceRecords.notes: Used only to establish that the Cochrane review of ACT (originally reporting that ACT increased contact with services and reduced hospital admission relative to standard care) was withdrawn from publication in 2011, which is why the lesson rests current ACT claims on the 2017 intensive case management review, on earlier systematic reviews, and on program standards. Record title begins 'WITHDRAWN:'. No text reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Models of community care for severe mental illness: a review of research on case management (Schizophrenia Bulletin, 24(1), 37-74)
sourceRecords.provider: Mueser KT, Bond GR, Drake RE, Resnick SG / Oxford University Press
sourceRecords.notes: Abstract verified on the publisher page and cross-checked against the Europe PMC record (PMID 9502546). Supports: review of 75 studies; ACT and intensive case management reduce time in hospital and improve housing stability, especially among high service users; moderate effects on symptoms and quality of life; little effect on social functioning, arrests and time in jail, or vocational functioning; deterioration of gains when ACT or ICM services are reduced or withdrawn. Full text paywalled; only abstract-level findings are used.

sourceRecords.title: Effectiveness of different models of case management for substance-abusing populations (Journal of Psychoactive Drugs, 39(1), 81-95)
sourceRecords.provider: Vanderplasschen W, Wolf J, Rapp RC, Broekaert E / Taylor & Francis; bibliographic record and abstract retrieved through the Europe PMC REST API (EMBL-EBI)
sourceRecords.notes: Systematic review of 48 peer-reviewed articles (1993-2003). Supports the four-model taxonomy used in substance use services (intensive case management, assertive community treatment, strengths-based case management, generalist case management) and the model-specific findings: ICM and ACT supported for homeless and dually diagnosed populations; strengths-based and generalist models relatively effective for substance users generally; reduced inpatient service use, greater community service use, longer treatment retention and improved quality of life, with mixed results on drug use and psychosocial functioning. Abstract-level use only; PMID 17523588.

sourceRecords.title: Assertive Community Treatment (ACT) Teams Guidelines (2025)
sourceRecords.provider: New York State Office of Mental Health
sourceRecords.notes: Read in full via local PDF text extraction. Supports the structural specification of ACT: multidisciplinary team, in vivo services, a 10:1 caseload ratio, shared caseload with team-level responsibility, services for as long as needed, flexible delivery via daily team meetings, and availability 24 hours a day 7 days a week; admission indicators including two or more psychiatric inpatient admissions in 12 months or one hospitalization of 60 days or more; assessment as an ongoing process reviewed at least every six months and reconsidered after significant events; daily team meeting review of hospitalizations, incarcerations, risk and emerging needs; transition and discharge planning; documentation and progress-note requirements tied to reimbursement; and required staff competence in person-centered language and cultural humility. No reuse licence stated; described in original wording.

sourceRecords.title: Uses of strength-based interventions for people with serious mental illness: A critical review (International Journal of Social Psychiatry, 62(3), 281-291)
sourceRecords.provider: Tse, S., Tsoi, E. W. S., Hamilton, B., O'Hagan, M., Shepherd, G., Slade, M., Whitley, R., & Petrakis, M. / SAGE
sourceRecords.notes: Reused source record (identical id and URL already in the phase-1 registry). Cited here only for the evidence status of the strengths model of case management: emerging evidence of benefit across seven intervention studies alongside the authors' call for higher-quality research. The strengths perspective itself is taught in the Strengths-Based Practice lesson, not here.

sourceRecords.title: The strengths based approach as a service delivery model for severe mental illness: a meta-analysis of clinical trials (BMC Psychiatry, 14:243)
sourceRecords.provider: Ibrahim, N., Michail, M., & Callaghan, P. / BMC Psychiatry
sourceRecords.notes: Reused source record (identical id and URL already in the phase-1 registry). Cited here for the counterweight to Tse: five pooled studies with 194 participants and no significant effect on level of functioning or quality of life, which is why the lesson treats the strengths model as one model among several with unsettled evidence.

sourceRecords.title: Does it matter how we refer to individuals with substance-related conditions? A randomized study of two commonly used terms (International Journal of Drug Policy, 21(3), 202-207)
sourceRecords.provider: Kelly, J. F., & Westerhoff, C. M. / Elsevier
sourceRecords.notes: Reused source record (identical id and URL already in the phase-1 registry). Supports the lesson's language section: in a randomized comparison of otherwise identical vignettes, the labeling term produced greater attribution of personal responsibility and more punitive judgments among clinicians. Used to show that terminology has measurable effects on professional judgment, not merely on etiquette.

sourceRecords.title: Words Matter: Preferred Language for Talking About Addiction
sourceRecords.provider: National Institute on Drug Abuse, National Institutes of Health
sourceRecords.notes: Reused source record (identical id and URL already in the phase-1 registry). Supports the statement that federal guidance now recommends describing the condition or behavior rather than labeling the person, and that stigmatizing terms affect how people are treated and how they see themselves.
